newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission seeks clearer powers over air pacts.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission seeks clearer powers over air pacts.

text.p: The European Commission said on Tuesday that it had proposed legislation giving it clear and indisputable jurisdiction over alliances between EU and non-EU airlines.

The draft rules, which had been expected for two weeks, came as the Commission informed the British authorities of its final conclusions on the proposed link-up between British Airways and AMR's American Airlines.
The spokesman for European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said this was a coincidence.
"The text is not linked to the BA-American alliance. It's pure chance in terms of calendar," Willy Helin told the Commission's daily news briefing.

Van Miert met British Trade and Industry Secretary Margaret Beckett on Tuesday. A Commission source said before the meeting he was expected to say that the proposed agreement would harm competition as it stands particularly between the United States and Britain.
According to a 1987 EU regulation on air transport, the Commission has clear authority to probe deals affecting only services between EU airports.

The Commission has long sought to extend the rules to deals with airlines based outside the EU. It believes it may now get the support of a majority of national governments due to the liberalisation of the bloc's air transport sector and to the mushrooming of transatlantic alliances.

Britain argued earlier this year it, not the Commission, has jurisdiction under article 88 of the treaty of Rome to investigate the alliance between British Airways and American. The Commission has equally asserted its right to vet the deal under article 89 and a string of other legal instruments.
After an open confrontation between the two authorities in January, the mood has been more cooperative, lawyers and EU sources said.
The German authorities have also started their own probe into a deal between Lufthansa, SAS and United Airlines, which is also being vetted in Brussels, but have not challenged the EU's authority.

The Commission proposed to modify the air transport regulation in 1989 but ran into opposition from almost all EU countries jealous of their sovereignty over a sector still dominated by state-controlled flag carriers.

"This time it ought to be a lot easier," Helin said, although he acknowledged that the new rules would probably come too late to bring the BA-American and other international alliances unequivocally under the Commission's wing.
The Commission said in a statement on Tuesday that the revised regulation would be good for airlines which would have the "advantage of a single control on the legality of their agreements".
While debate continues about the division of vetting labours on the eastern side of the Atlantic, the U.S. Department of Transportation is also scrutinising the planned deal's effects.
